titre: Dracula (1931) has a Spanish version shot at night on the same sets
accroche: By day, Tod Browning films Bela Lugosi. By night, on the same stages, another crew shoots another Dracula, in Spanish.
contenu_vulgarise:
On October 10, 1930, on a stage at Universal Studios, Tod Browning shoots Dracula with Bela Lugosi. When night falls, a second crew takes over the same sets, with a different director, George Melford, and different actors, including Carlos Villarías in the title role and Lupita Tovar. It shoots the same script, in Spanish.

## One stock of film, two movies

Dubbing doesn't exist yet in 1930. To sell a talking picture outside English-speaking countries, the Hollywood studios shoot foreign-language versions, often at night, on sets already built for the original version, on a tighter budget. The practice, which disappears within a few years with the arrival of dubbing, then affects most big talking productions: Universal, like the other studios, shoots Spanish, French or German versions of its best-selling films in parallel. Melford thus directs his own crew for twenty-two days, in parallel with Browning's shooting schedule. He has a clear advantage: every morning, he watches the dailies shot the day before by the day crew, and adjusts his own shots accordingly, on scenes he hasn't yet filmed. Villarías doesn't have that freedom: the only member of the Spanish cast allowed to see Browning's footage, he has to use it to imitate Bela Lugosi's performance rather than to depart from it. The director innovates, the lead actor copies. The result, twenty-nine minutes longer than the original (104 minutes against 75), develops dialogue cut on the English side, and moves the camera more than Browning's, which stayed essentially static.

## What this shifts

The Spanish version disappears from screens after its release, relegated to the status of an export byproduct. An incomplete print resurfaces in a New Jersey warehouse in the 1970s; it takes the discovery of a complete print at the Cinemateca de Cuba, in Havana, for the film to be restored in full. The film historian David J. Skal, in Hollywood Gothic (1990), judges it superior to Browning's. In 2015, it in turn joins the Library of Congress's National Film Registry, alongside the English original that had eclipsed it for more than forty years. The film conceived as the budget version, shot in the other's shadow, ended up surpassing it.

repere.texte: The Spanish version of Dracula runs one hundred four minutes, against seventy-five for Tod Browning's English version shot in parallel on the same sets. The historian David J. Skal judges it, in Hollywood Gothic (1990), superior to the English original.
repere.source: David J. Skal, Hollywood Gothic: The Tangled Web of Dracula from Novel to Stage to Screen, Norton, 1990

carte.punch: The real Dracula shot in Spanish in 1930 runs 29 minutes longer, on the same sets.
carte.idee: While Tod Browning shoots Dracula with Bela Lugosi by day, another crew uses the same sets at night to shoot a Spanish version. Twenty-nine minutes longer, it is now judged by historians to be superior to the original, and joins the National Film Registry in 2015.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: A shot-by-shot comparison of the two versions, English and Spanish, shot on the same sets.

quiz.question: Why does the Spanish version of Dracula (1931), shot at night on the same sets as Tod Browning's, run 29 minutes longer than the English original?
choix: Because Universal imposed a longer running time on versions meant for export
Because George Melford, watching the previous day's dailies every morning, develops scenes cut on the English side
Because the film stock used at night required a slower projection speed
Because the Spanish actors improvised more, lacking a script as polished as the original
quiz.explication: Nothing indicates an export running-time directive, a different film stock, or actors left to improvise, when Carlos Villarías, on the contrary, was supposed to imitate Bela Lugosi. The difference lies in the shoot itself: Melford saw Browning's dailies every morning, and took advantage of them to flesh out scenes and dialogue cut on the English side.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Among the actors in the Spanish cast of the 1930 Dracula, who was the only one allowed to watch the footage shot by Tod Browning's crew?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says Villarías was the only member of the Spanish cast allowed to see Browning's dailies, to imitate Lugosi's performance; Melford, who also watched them, was the director, not an actor, and Tovar and Lugosi did not have this access.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where was the complete print of the Spanish version of Dracula found, allowing its full restoration?
choix: At the Cinemateca de Cuba, in Havana
In the archives of the Library of Congress
quiz_supplementaire.explication: An incomplete print had resurfaced in a New Jersey warehouse in the 1970s, but only the discovery of a complete print at the Cinemateca de Cuba made the film's full restoration possible.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the film historian David J. Skal say, in Hollywood Gothic (1990), about the Spanish version of Dracula?
choix: That it owes its success to a bigger budget than Browning's
That it was shot before the English version
That it is a byproduct of no artistic interest
That it is superior to Tod Browning's English version
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Skal judges the Spanish version superior to Browning's; it had, on the contrary, a tighter budget, was not an immediate success, and was shot in parallel with, not before, the English one.
